client: I've been really struggling since my dad passed away two months ago. Every time I go to a family gathering, it just hits me all over again — I see his empty chair, or someone mentions something he used to say, and I completely fall apart. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to make any difference, because it's not like anything can actually bring him back.
therapist: What you're carrying right now is immense — the grief in your words and even in the quietness of your voice tells me how deeply you loved your dad, and how raw this still is. You're right that nothing will bring him back, and I want to honor that truth rather than minimize it. And while talking can't change that loss, it can gently help you find ways to carry it that feel a little less like falling apart — would you be willing to explore that together?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, fast speech

client: I guess I'm willing to try, but I'm honestly not sure how much good it'll do. It's not like I can just stop going to family things — my mom needs me there, and skipping would probably make me feel even worse about myself. But every time I walk through that door and see his chair, it's like the loss is brand new all over again.
therapist: There's something really meaningful in the fact that you keep showing up for your mom even when it costs you so much — that speaks to the kind of person you are, and likely the kind of relationship you had with your dad too. The way you're describing that moment at the door, it sounds like your mind and body are treating each family gathering as a fresh encounter with the loss, almost like a wound that doesn't get the chance to start healing. One thing we might gently explore together is whether there's a small way to prepare yourself for that moment — not to avoid the grief, but to give it a little more room so it doesn't hit you quite so suddenly.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, but I honestly don't know what "preparing myself" would even look like in practice. Like, do I just sit in my car beforehand and tell myself it's going to hurt? Because I've tried that kind of thing before and when the moment actually comes, it doesn't matter what I told myself — I still end up crying in the bathroom. It feels like my body just takes over no matter what I do.
therapist: The way you're speaking — softly, but with your thoughts racing — tells me this feels both exhausting and a little hopeless right now, like you've already tried to fight this and lost. I want to gently reframe something though: crying in the bathroom isn't your body betraying you or proof that nothing works — it's actually your love for your dad finding the only exit it can in that moment. What if instead of trying to *stop* that from happening, we explored ways to be a little kinder to yourself when it does — so it feels less like falling apart, and more like something you can move through?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That framing actually caught me off guard a little — I've never thought of it as love finding an exit, I've mostly just felt embarrassed and weak when it happens. But I'm not sure what "being kinder to myself" actually means in those moments, because when I'm standing there trying to hold it together, I'm not exactly in a headspace where I can coach myself through anything. It's like the grief just swallows me whole before I even have a chance to think.
therapist: The way you just said that — there's something that shifted slightly, like a small crack of openness alongside the pain, and I want to stay with that. You're right that in the middle of being swallowed by grief, there's no room for a pep talk — so "being kinder to yourself" might actually happen *before* and *after* the moment, not during it, like giving yourself permission afterward to say "that was hard, and I got through it" instead of "I fell apart again." That small shift in the story you tell yourself after — from weakness to love, from failure to survival — is actually where a lot of healing can quietly begin.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I want to believe that could work, but I'm worried that in the moment after, when I'm washing my face in the bathroom mirror, I'm just going to feel that same rush of shame before I can catch myself and reframe anything. It's like the shame is faster than the rational thought. I guess I'm also carrying this guilt that I should be stronger for my mom — she lost her husband, and here I am falling apart when she needs me to hold things together.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — quickly, with an urgency in your voice — tells me this guilt about your mom is pressing down on you heavily, almost like you've added a second weight on top of the grief itself. I want to gently challenge something though: is it possible that your mom, who also loved your dad deeply, might actually feel *less* alone seeing that you're hurting too, rather than let down by it? The idea that you need to be the strong one might feel like loyalty to your family, but it could also be a quiet way of being very hard on yourself at the exact moment you deserve the most gentleness.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: That actually made me tear up a little, because there was this one moment at the last gathering where my mom and I just looked at each other across the table and both started crying at the same time, and honestly it didn't feel awful — it felt like we were in it together. But I think I've been telling myself that was a failure on my part, like I let her down in that moment, when maybe it wasn't that at all. I'm just so used to thinking I need to be the one holding things together that I don't even know how to let myself off the hook for being human.
therapist: The way you're speaking — softly, with a kind of tender urgency — tells me that memory with your mom is actually really precious to you, even if you've been filing it under "failure." What you just described wasn't a breakdown — it was a moment of genuine human connection, two people who loved the same man, finding each other in the pain. I wonder if that moment might actually be worth holding onto as *evidence* against the story that you need to be strong for her — because it sounds like what she may need most is simply *you*, not a version of you that's holding everything together.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: When you put it that way, it's hard to argue with, because that moment with my mom was actually one of the only times in the past two months where I didn't feel completely alone in this. But I think part of me is scared to hold onto it as evidence, because what if I start letting myself off the hook and then I actually do fail her when she really needs me — like, what if allowing myself to be human just becomes an excuse to fall apart at the wrong moment? I don't fully trust myself to know where that line is.
therapist: The speed and pitch in your voice right now tells me this fear is very alive for you — like you're already bracing for a version of yourself that doesn't exist yet. But I want to gently point something out: the very fact that you're this worried about failing your mom is itself evidence that you won't — people who truly don't care don't lie awake afraid of letting others down. Giving yourself permission to be human isn't the same as giving up your love for her; those two things can exist together, and learning to trust that is something we can work on slowly, together.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That actually lands differently than I expected it to — like, I've never thought of my worry itself as proof that I care, I've just experienced it as this constant low-level dread that I'm not doing enough. But I'm still a little skeptical, because caring a lot and actually being enough for someone aren't the same thing, and I don't want to use that logic as a way to feel better when maybe I genuinely do need to step up more. I guess I just don't fully trust my own judgment right now when everything still feels so raw and unstable.
therapist: The quickness in your voice and the way your thoughts are moving fast tells me your mind is working very hard right now — almost like it doesn't quite trust itself to rest on anything that feels like relief. Your skepticism is actually healthy and worth honoring — caring deeply *and* sometimes falling short are both true, and I'm not asking you to pretend otherwise. But I'd gently offer this: right now, two months into one of the hardest losses a person can face, "not fully trusting your judgment" isn't a character flaw — it's just what grief does, and it won't always feel this raw and unstable.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think what's getting to me is that "it won't always feel this raw" — because I've been telling myself that too, but two months in it still feels just as sharp as the first week, so part of me has started to wonder if this is just who I am now. Like maybe I'm someone who doesn't heal the way other people do, and I'm scared to hope that it'll get easier in case it doesn't and I've just been fooling myself. I don't know if that makes sense, but the idea of hoping feels almost more dangerous than just staying braced for the worst.
therapist: The way you're speaking — very quickly, with a kind of tightness in your voice — tells me this fear runs really deep, like part of you is already grieving the possibility of healing itself. What you're describing has a name in CBT: it's called "protective pessimism," where hope starts to feel more threatening than pain because at least pain is familiar and won't surprise you. But I want to gently offer this: the fact that grief still feels sharp at two months isn't evidence that you're broken or different from others — it's evidence that your dad mattered enormously, and two months is still very, very early in learning to carry a love that has nowhere left to go.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: "Protective pessimism" — I've never heard it put that way before, but it does feel uncomfortably accurate, like you just named something I've been doing without realizing it. I think part of me has been treating staying braced as a kind of loyalty to my dad, like if I start to heal or hope, it means I'm moving on from him, and that feels like a betrayal. I don't know how to want to get better without it feeling like I'm leaving him behind.
therapist: The way you're speaking — quickly, with a kind of breathless urgency — tells me this realization is hitting you somewhere very deep and true, like you've just uncovered something that's been quietly running in the background for months. I want to offer you something important: healing doesn't mean leaving your dad behind — it means learning to carry him *with* you rather than staying frozen at the place where you lost him, and those are very different things. The love doesn't go anywhere; it just slowly finds a new shape, and wanting that for yourself isn't betrayal — it might actually be one of the most faithful things you can do for who he was to you.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech
